newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-British Steel braced for H1 stress.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-British Steel braced for H1 stress.

text.p: British Steel is poised to report a sharp drop in first-half profits on Monday, hit by falling steel prices and a strong pound, analysts said.

"Product pricing is still a major (negative) factor and although volumes have kept going and some prices have stopped falling...the falls there have been, especially in stainless steel, have been sharp in the last year," Peter Caldwell, steel analyst at Nikko Europe said on Friday. On average analysts expected pretax profit to be more than halved to 258 million stg from 550 million stg a year ago.

The interim dividend is widely expected to be unchanged from last time at three pence, with the group's net cash surplus of some 600 million stg and accumulated dividend cover providing the market with some comfort.
Earnings per share for the full year 1997 are now forecast by 22 analysts -- surveyed by Edinburgh Financial -- to decline to 21 pence from 38 pence in 1996.

But analysts said the outlook for the second half could be brighter. The market hopes British Steel chairman Brian Moffat will say the over-stocking situation has improved, which will help the company secure better prices in the second half.
The share price is now around 170 pence, well off a year high of 201-1/2 and underperforming the FT-All Share index by 14 percent and the FT Engineering sector by 13 percent since October.
But analysts say much of the bad news is factored into the price.

"These are tough times for British Steel. While the volumes and order books are reasonably good especially after the de-stocking, there's a currency issue here," said Tony Lancelott, steel analyst at UBS Ltd.

In addition to currency risk, the group still faces the cyclical problem of over-supply and sagging demand. US steel output is anticpated by SG Warburg to be up 19 percent by 1998 and South East Asian production to be up 39 percent while global steel consumption shows only a slight increase.

News on Friday that Avesta Sheffield, 51-percent-owned by British Steel, had its first-half profits almost entirely wiped out by low stainless steel prices and losses in inventories does not bode well for the group's overall earnings.

"Inevitably it will mean that British Steel will not have any contribution from Avesta or only a very slight contribution from it in the first half. So whether they made up for that in their own business, we'll see," Lancelott said
British Steel's stake in Avesta Sheffield boosted its full year profits last June by 228 million stg. It is still unclear whether it will up its stake in the Swedish unit.
Avesta said it expected further price increases in some of its products to help lift profitability, but it could not say what the pace of recovery would be.
Avesta's production volumes had been hit by stock building which, it said, was being "progressively reversed" so that stocks were nearing a level consistent with real demand.
